questions.q: What was the name of the female allegorical figure that represented the French nation?
questions.explanation: Marianne was the popular female figure symbolising the French nation; Germania represented Germany.

questions.q: Garibaldi’s volunteer force in the Italian unification wars was popularly known as the
questions.explanation: Giuseppe Garibaldi led the Red Shirts, who helped to win southern Italy in 1860.

questions.q: After Napoleon’s defeat at Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna restored which dynasty to the throne of France?
questions.explanation: The Bourbon dynasty, overthrown during the French Revolution, was restored in France in 1815.

questions.q: The Greek struggle for independence, which began in 1821, was fought against which empire?
questions.explanation: Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire; it was recognised as independent by the Treaty of Constantinople in 1832.

questions.q: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 fail to unite Germany?
options: The Prussian king rejected the crown it offered, and the monarchy and army opposed it
It was banned by the Pope
questions.explanation: King Frederick William IV of Prussia refused the crown, and the monarchy, army and landowners joined forces to end the Parliament.

questions.q: Why was the Balkan region a source of tension in the late 19th century?
options: It had no people living in it
It was ruled by a single powerful nation-state
Ottoman rule was weakening, Slavic peoples sought independence, and European powers competed for influence there
It was the only part of Europe with industries
questions.explanation: Nationalist aspirations and rivalry among the great powers made the Balkans a region of conflict that helped lead to the First World War.

questions.q: What did the female figures Marianne and Germania stand for?
questions.answer: They were allegories, that is, a person standing for an abstract idea. Marianne personified the French nation and Germania the German nation, so that people could picture and feel loyalty to the idea of the nation.
keyPoints: Marianne for France and Germania for Germany
Helped people identify with the nation
questions.explanation: Artists used such figures to give a face to an abstract idea.

questions.q: Explain how Napoleon’s administrative reforms made life easier for businessmen and traders.
questions.answer: Napoleon removed internal customs barriers, introduced uniform weights and measures and a common national currency, and improved transport and communication. This made it easier to move and trade goods across the territory.
questions.explanation: A common system lowered the cost and difficulty of doing business.

questions.q: Who presided over the Lahore Congress session of December 1929, which declared Purna Swaraj as the goal?
questions.explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru presided at Lahore, and 26 January 1930 was to be celebrated as Independence Day.

questions.q: The slogan ‘Do or Die’ is associated with which movement?
questions.explanation: Gandhiji gave the call ‘Do or Die’ at the launch of the Quit India Movement in August 1942.

questions.q: Gandhiji’s first Satyagraha in India in 1917, on behalf of indigo cultivators, took place at
questions.explanation: In Champaran in Bihar he supported peasants who were forced by planters to grow indigo.

questions.q: The Swaraj Party was formed within the Congress by
options: Subhas Chandra Bose and Jawaharlal Nehru
C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru
questions.explanation: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923 to argue for a return to council politics.

questions.q: Why did many Indian industrialists support the Civil Disobedience Movement?
options: They wanted all trade with Britain stopped immediately
They were forced to by the government
They wanted to end colonial control over the economy and obtain protection against imports
questions.explanation: Industrialists wanted protection against imported goods and freedom from colonial restrictions on business.

questions.q: Why did Dr B. R. Ambedkar demand separate electorates for the Depressed Classes?
options: To make sure that their representatives would be chosen by Dalit voters themselves
To give them control over the army
questions.explanation: Ambedkar feared that general electorates would choose representatives who did not reflect the interests of the Depressed Classes.

questions.q: What did Gandhiji mean by Satyagraha?
questions.answer: Satyagraha means the force of truth. It is a method of non-violent resistance in which people refuse to obey unjust laws, accepting suffering without hatred, to appeal to the conscience of the oppressor and win the cause by moral strength.
keyPoints: Appeal to conscience, not physical force
questions.explanation: Satyagraha was Gandhiji’s method of mass struggle.

questions.q: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement spread in the towns?
questions.answer: Middle-class people left government schools and colleges, lawyers gave up legal practice, and councils were boycotted. Foreign cloth was boycotted and burnt, and the use of khadi and Indian goods rose, though the movement slowed as khadi was costlier.
keyPoints: Boycott of schools, courts and councils
Use of khadi and Indian goods
questions.explanation: The movement combined political boycott with economic self-reliance.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The cattle disease that devastated Africa in the 1890s was called
questions.explanation: Rinderpest killed most of the cattle in Africa and weakened people’s ability to resist European rule.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In which year did the First World War begin?
questions.explanation: The First World War began in 1914 and ended in 1918.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which organisation, formed in 1995, took over the work of GATT?
questions.explanation: The World Trade Organization replaced GATT in 1995 to set rules for international trade.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: After slavery was abolished in British colonies, plantation owners increasingly turned to
options: indentured labourers brought in from India and elsewhere
questions.explanation: Indentured labour from places such as India filled the labour gap on plantations.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: In the nineteenth century, how did the pattern of India’s trade change under British rule?
options: India exported machinery and imported raw cotton
India became a supplier of raw materials such as raw cotton and indigo and a buyer of British manufactured goods
India exported finished cotton cloth in ever larger quantities to Britain
questions.explanation: Cheap British factory goods flooded India while raw materials were exported to feed British industry.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why did newly independent developing countries demand a New International Economic Order (NIEO) after the Second World War?
options: They wanted to join the League of Nations
They had no resources to trade
They felt the IMF and World Bank mainly served industrial powers and wanted better terms of trade
questions.explanation: Developing countries sought control over their natural resources and fairer trade terms, forming the Group of 77.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did the First World War affect the world economy?
questions.answer: The war caused huge destruction and debt. Britain borrowed heavily from the US, which changed from a debtor to a creditor nation. War industries expanded and, after the war, it was hard for Europe to regain its earlier trade and prosperity.
questions.explanation: The war shifted economic power towards the United States.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did railways, steamships and refrigeration change food trade in the nineteenth century?
questions.answer: Railways and steamships moved food faster and more cheaply over long distances. Refrigerated ships let meat and dairy products travel from distant lands to Europe, so food prices fell and diets changed.
keyPoints: Refrigeration allowed perishable goods to travel
questions.explanation: New technology made global food trade possible.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Who invented the spinning jenny in 1764?
questions.explanation: James Hargreaves’s spinning jenny allowed one worker to spin several threads at once.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Near which city was India’s first jute mill set up in 1855?
questions.explanation: The first jute mill was set up near Calcutta, in Bengal.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: In the woollen trade, a stapler was a person who
options: sorted wool according to its fibre
questions.explanation: A stapler sorted wool by staple or fibre before it was cleaned and spun.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Labels placed on cloth by Manchester manufacturers helped to show
options: the place of manufacture and the quality of the goods
questions.explanation: Labels carried the name of the firm and place, assuring buyers of quality.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did handloom weaving survive in India despite competition from mills?
options: Mills were unable to spin any yarn
Weavers adopted improvements such as the fly shuttle and mills mostly made coarse cloth, leaving room for weavers
questions.explanation: Technical improvements, and the fact that mills concentrated on coarse varieties, helped many weavers survive.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why were many hand-spinners in Britain unhappy about the spinning jenny?
options: It did the work with less labour, leaving many women without jobs
questions.explanation: The jenny reduced the need for hand spinners, so many women lost their income and sometimes attacked the machines.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Describe the working conditions of early factory workers in Britain.
questions.answer: Workers, including women and children, put in long hours for low wages. Jobs were uncertain, housing in towns was crowded and unsanitary, and there was little protection from accidents.
questions.explanation: Rapid growth of towns outpaced facilities for workers.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: How did the First World War help the growth of industries in India?
questions.answer: British mills were busy making goods for the war, so imports to India declined and Indian mills found a larger home market. Indian factories also supplied war needs such as jute bags, cloth for uniforms and tents, and production and working hours increased.
keyPoints: Bigger home market for Indian goods
questions.explanation: The war gave Indian industry a chance to expand.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: The oldest Japanese book, printed in 868 CE, was the
questions.explanation: The Buddhist Diamond Sutra is the oldest Japanese book printed using woodblocks.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Who wrote the book Gulamgiri, published in 1871, criticising caste injustice?
questions.explanation: Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri, a book against caste oppression.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Raja Ram Mohan Roy’s journal Sambad Kaumudi (1821) mainly
options: supported reform ideas, including opposition to the practice of sati
questions.explanation: Roy used print to argue for social reform.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Raja Ravi Varma is remembered for
options: paintings of gods and goddesses that were reproduced in cheap prints and sold widely
building the first press in Goa
questions.explanation: His pictures, printed in large numbers, brought images of deities into many homes.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print help women in nineteenth-century India?
options: It enabled women to read, write and publish, including journals and autobiographies
It made schools compulsory for all girls overnight
questions.explanation: Women began writing about their lives and views; Rassundari Debi’s Amar Jiban is an early example.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Why did newspapers play an important part in India’s national movement?
options: They were controlled by the colonial government
They reported colonial misrule and spread nationalist ideas, helping people to unite
questions.explanation: Nationalist papers criticised British policy and encouraged a sense of unity.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: What was woodblock printing, and how did it reach Europe?
questions.answer: In woodblock printing, text or images are carved on a wooden block, inked and pressed on paper. It developed in China, and Marco Polo brought the knowledge to Italy after his travels in the late 13th century.
keyPoints: Marco Polo brought it to Italy
questions.explanation: Woodblock printing was the first printing method in Europe.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print help the reform movements in nineteenth-century India?
questions.answer: Reformers published books, pamphlets and journals to spread their ideas on social issues such as caste, the status of women and religion. They could reach large audiences and spark public debate; examples include Roy’s journal and Phule’s Gulamgiri.
keyPoints: Spread reformers’ ideas to many readers
Public debate on caste, women and religion
Examples such as Gulamgiri or Sambad Kaumudi
questions.explanation: Print made public discussion of social issues possible.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Coal takes millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly.

questions.q: Which landform covers the largest share of India’s area, about 43 per cent?
questions.explanation: Plains cover about 43 per cent, mountains about 30 per cent and plateaus about 27 per cent.

questions.q: Which soil gets its reddish colour from iron compounds in crystalline rocks?
questions.explanation: Red soil develops on crystalline igneous rocks and its colour comes from iron.

questions.q: The newer, more fertile alluvium in river plains is called
questions.explanation: Khadar is the newer alluvium; the older alluvium is bangar.

questions.q: Over-irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh has led to land degradation mainly through
options: waterlogging and increasing salinity of the soil
questions.explanation: Too much irrigation raises the water table and brings salts to the surface, reducing fertility.

questions.q: Why is resource planning especially important in a country like India?
options: Resources are unevenly distributed, so careful planning is needed for balanced use
All resources are equal in every region
questions.explanation: Some regions are rich in minerals while others are rich in water or soil, so planning helps balance development.

questions.q: Name any four main types of soil found in India.
questions.answer: The main soils are alluvial, black, red and yellow, laterite, arid and forest soils.
keyPoints: Laterite or arid or forest soil
questions.explanation: Soils differ by parent rock, climate and rainfall.

questions.q: Explain how shelter belts and strip cropping help check soil erosion.
questions.answer: Shelter belts are rows of trees planted to break the force of the wind, protecting soil in dry areas. In strip cropping, strips of crops are separated by grass, which slows wind and water and reduces the loss of topsoil.
keyPoints: Shelter belts: trees break the wind
Strip cropping: grass strips between crops
questions.explanation: Both methods reduce the force of wind or water on bare soil.

questions.q: Rice is mainly a
questions.explanation: Rice is sown with the monsoon and harvested in autumn, so it is a kharif crop.

questions.q: Which crop is known as the ‘golden fibre’?
questions.explanation: Jute is called the golden fibre because of its colour and value.

questions.q: Which crop is grown both for food and as fodder, mainly in the kharif season?
questions.explanation: Maize is used as food and fodder.

questions.q: Operation Flood, also called the White Revolution, was related to
questions.explanation: Operation Flood aimed to increase milk production in India through cooperatives.

questions.q: Why is water scarcity in India not only the result of low rainfall?
options: Over-exploitation, unequal access and rising demand from a growing population and industry also cause it
questions.explanation: Even regions with enough rain face shortage because of overuse and unequal distribution.

questions.q: Why is drip irrigation suitable for dry regions?
options: It needs more labour than other methods
It delivers water directly to plant roots, reducing evaporation and waste
It is useful only in deserts without plants
questions.explanation: Delivering water slowly near roots saves water.

questions.q: Write two differences between subsistence agriculture and commercial agriculture.
questions.answer: In subsistence agriculture farmers grow crops mainly for their own families, on small plots with simple tools and family labour. In commercial agriculture crops are grown for sale in the market, using more machines, chemicals and capital.
keyPoints: Subsistence: for own use, small plots, simple tools
Commercial: for sale, more modern inputs and capital
questions.explanation: The key difference is the purpose of cultivation and the inputs used.

questions.q: Explain two benefits and two problems of large multipurpose dams.
questions.answer: Dams store water for irrigation, generate hydroelectricity, help control floods and supply water for towns. They can displace communities, submerge forests and farmland, and disturb river ecosystems.
keyPoints: Benefits such as irrigation, electricity, flood control
Problems such as displacement and loss of forest and land
questions.explanation: Dams bring benefits but also social and environmental costs.

questions.q: Which mineral is the chief raw material for making aluminium?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is extracted from bauxite.

questions.q: Digboi in Assam is known for its
questions.explanation: Digboi is one of India’s oldest oil-producing areas.

questions.q: Which mineral occurs in sheets and is widely used as an insulator in electrical goods?
questions.explanation: Mica resists heat and electricity, so it is used in electrical and electronic goods.

questions.q: Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is known for large deposits of
questions.explanation: Neyveli has big deposits of lignite, also called brown coal.

questions.q: Why is solar energy considered suitable for India?
options: It is very costly to maintain
It is useful only at night
Most of the country receives plenty of sunshine through the year, and it is clean and renewable
questions.explanation: Abundant sunshine and no pollution make solar power attractive.

questions.q: Which combination of factors helped the growth of cotton textile mills in Maharashtra and Gujarat?
options: Availability of raw cotton and nearby ports for trade
questions.explanation: Cotton from the black-soil region and ports such as Bombay supported the industry.

questions.q: Mention any three factors that influence the location of an industry.
questions.answer: Important factors include availability of raw material, power, labour, capital, transport and market, and government policies.
questions.explanation: Industries are set up where costs are low and access to markets is good.

questions.q: Suggest two measures each to control water and air pollution caused by industries.
questions.answer: For water: treat effluents before discharge and reuse water in processes. For air: install smoke filters or precipitators in chimneys and use cleaner fuels such as natural gas.
questions.explanation: Treating waste and cutting emissions at the source reduces pollution.

questions.q: Which of these countries has a federal system?
questions.explanation: The USA divides power between a national government and state governments.

questions.q: The third tier of government in India is
questions.explanation: Local governments such as panchayats and municipalities form the third tier.

questions.q: Which body settles disputes between the Union and the states over the division of powers in India?
options: The judiciary, headed by the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The courts interpret the Constitution and settle disputes over powers.

questions.q: Subjects that do not fall in any of the three lists, called residuary subjects, lie with the
questions.explanation: In India, residuary powers rest with the Union government.

questions.q: Why is power shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary (horizontal division) useful?
options: It makes all decisions by a single organ
Each organ checks the others, so none can exercise unlimited power
It removes the need for a constitution
questions.explanation: Checks and balances prevent misuse of power.

questions.q: Why is local government important for democracy?
options: It is needed only in cities
Decisions on local issues can be taken close to the people, which increases participation
questions.explanation: People understand local problems best, and local bodies give them a direct role in solving them.

questions.q: What is federalism? Mention two features of a federal system.
questions.answer: Federalism is a system in which power is divided between a central authority and its constituent units. There are two or more levels of government with their own areas, the powers of each are defined in the constitution, and neither level can unilaterally change this arrangement.
keyPoints: Power divided between central and state governments
questions.explanation: In a federation each level of government has its own sphere of authority.

questions.q: Why did the majoritarian policies of Sri Lanka lead to conflict?
questions.answer: After independence, Sinhala was made the only official language and Sinhala applicants were favoured for jobs and university places. Tamils felt neglected and discriminated against, sought autonomy, and the tension grew into a long civil conflict.
keyPoints: Sinhala made the only official language
Preference to Sinhala speakers in jobs and education
Tamils felt alienated and sought autonomy
questions.explanation: Ignoring the needs of a minority can fuel conflict.

questions.q: Who described democracy as a government ‘of the people, by the people, for the people’?
questions.explanation: Abraham Lincoln used this description in his Gettysburg Address.

questions.q: Which body conducts elections to Parliament and State Legislatures in India?
questions.explanation: The Election Commission is an independent body that supervises elections.

questions.q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability?
questions.explanation: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence.

questions.q: A secular state is one in which
options: there is an official state religion
the state has no official religion and treats all religions equally
questions.explanation: India is a secular country in which the state does not promote any religion.

questions.q: Why is reserving one-third of seats for women in local bodies important?
options: It reduces the powers of panchayats
It increases women’s participation in decision-making and representation
questions.explanation: Reservation brings more women into local politics and gives them a say in local decisions.

questions.q: Why is democracy considered more accountable than other forms of government?
options: Citizens can question rulers and change them through elections and public debate
questions.explanation: Regular elections and freedom to criticise make rulers answerable.

questions.q: Name the three components of a political party.
questions.answer: A political party has three components: the leaders, the active members, and the followers.
questions.explanation: These three groups together make up a party.

questions.q: How does democracy help to accommodate social diversity?
questions.answer: Democracy allows different groups to express their views and to share power through peaceful negotiation. Giving every community a voice and rights reduces the chance that differences turn into violent conflict.
keyPoints: Different groups can voice their views
questions.explanation: Democracies manage differences through dialogue and rights.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Manufacturing belongs to which sector of the economy?
questions.explanation: The secondary sector turns natural products into other goods through manufacturing.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: The Human Development Report is published by
questions.explanation: UNDP publishes the Human Development Report, which includes the Human Development Index.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Which of the following is a tertiary activity?
questions.explanation: Banking is a service, so it belongs to the tertiary sector.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Seasonal unemployment occurs when
options: people cannot find work in some months of the year
everyone works in the same factory
questions.explanation: Agricultural workers, for example, may find work only in sowing and harvesting seasons.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why must governments provide public facilities such as basic health and education?
options: Private firms never offer any services
They are essential for development and many poor people cannot afford them privately
They are not related to development
questions.explanation: Health and education improve quality of life, so governments need to make them available to all.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why has the tertiary sector’s share in GDP risen over time?
options: Services such as transport, trade and communication grow as incomes and needs rise
questions.explanation: As economies grow, demand for services such as banking, transport and ICT increases.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: What is the difference between the public sector and the private sector?
questions.answer: In the public sector the government owns most of the assets and provides services, as in railways and the post office. In the private sector ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of private individuals or companies, with the aim of profit.
keyPoints: Private: owned by individuals or companies
questions.explanation: The difference lies in who owns the assets.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why is sustainability important for development? Give an example.
questions.answer: Development that damages the environment or uses up resources cannot continue for long. For example, if groundwater is pumped out faster than it is recharged, the water table falls and future farming and drinking water supplies are endangered.
questions.explanation: Development should not reduce the resources available to future generations.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Money acts as
questions.explanation: Money is accepted in exchange for goods and services, which removes the need for barter.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Which mark certifies the purity of gold jewellery in India?
questions.explanation: Hallmarking certifies the purity of gold jewellery; ISI is for industrial products and Agmark for agricultural products.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: World Consumer Rights Day is observed on
questions.explanation: 15 March is World Consumer Rights Day; India observes National Consumer Day on 24 December.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Deposits in a bank that can be withdrawn on demand are called
questions.explanation: Money in a current or savings account can be withdrawn whenever needed, so it is called demand deposit.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why is formal credit generally better for the poor than informal credit?
options: It usually has lower interest rates and is supervised by the Reserve Bank, whereas informal lenders often charge very high interest
questions.explanation: High interest from informal lenders can trap borrowers in debt.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: How does the removal of trade barriers such as import taxes and quotas help globalisation?
options: It allows goods and investment to move more freely between countries
It raises the cost of imports
questions.explanation: Fewer barriers mean more trade and investment across borders.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: What is a Special Economic Zone (SEZ)?
questions.answer: An SEZ is an area set up to attract foreign and domestic companies, where they get facilities such as good infrastructure, tax benefits and relaxed rules, to encourage production and exports.
keyPoints: Aims to attract investment and exports
questions.explanation: SEZs are used to attract investment.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Explain how competition among producers benefits consumers but may also hurt small producers in a globalised economy.
questions.answer: Competition gives consumers more choice, better quality and lower prices. Small producers may not be able to match the costs of large companies, so some lose business or close.
keyPoints: More choice, better quality, lower prices
questions.explanation: Globalisation has benefits and costs depending on size and capacity.

questions.q: Who wrote the book Hind Swaraj in 1909?
questions.explanation: Hind Swaraj is Gandhiji’s 1909 book on swaraj and civilisation.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea with the
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

questions.q: The Constitution of India came into force in
questions.explanation: It came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Which sector is also known as the service sector?
questions.explanation: The tertiary sector provides services such as transport, banking and education.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Which Act of 2005 gives citizens the right to seek information from public authorities?
questions.explanation: The Right to Information Act, 2005, lets citizens ask for information from government departments.

questions.q: Rubber, an important plantation crop, is grown mainly in
questions.explanation: Rubber needs a moist, warm climate and is mostly grown in Kerala.

questions.q: Describe the Greek struggle for independence.
questions.answer: Greece was part of the Ottoman Empire. A struggle for independence began in 1821, supported by Greeks living abroad and by many West Europeans who admired ancient Greek culture. The Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation.
keyPoints: Support from Europeans who admired Greek culture
questions.explanation: The Greek struggle inspired nationalist movements elsewhere.

questions.q: State any three causes of soil erosion.
questions.answer: Soil erosion is caused by deforestation, overgrazing, heavy rain and running water, wind in dry areas, and unsuitable farming practices such as ploughing up and down slopes.
questions.explanation: Removal of the plant cover leaves soil exposed to wind and water.
